title: What USG is and what it does
content: The USC Undergraduate Student Government (USG) describes itself as the official governing body of over 20,000 undergraduates at the University of Southern California. Its stated purpose is to make the undergraduate experience the best it can be, and it pursues that through four kinds of work named on its About page: advocacy, legislative work, programming, and funding. USG is organized into three branches and four departments. The three branches are Executive (characterized on the page as leading the charge and bringing about change in the broader student community at USC), Legislative (directly representing student needs and concerns to all of USG and to USC through legislation and projects), and Judicial (ensuring the values of integrity, professionalism, and transparency in all of USG's operations). The four departments are Advocacy (working alongside administrators and campus partners to form policy and solve student issues), Communications (building a two-way bridge between USG, the student body, media, and registered student organizations), Funding (described on the page as disbursing nearly $350,000 for research, student organizations, and professional development), and Programming (organizing and executing dozens of entertaining, diverse, and educational events every week). The About page also publishes an organizational structure chart showing the departments and positions; the chart is labeled for 2023/24 and the page notes it was updated 8/31/25. Students with questions are invited to reach out to USG team members through the Meet Our Team page.

title: USG organizational structure: branches, departments, and officers
content: USG's published structure has two layers. First, three branches: Executive, Legislative, and Judicial. Second, four departments that carry out operational work: Advocacy, Communications, Funding, and Programming. The site places Communications, Programming, and Funding under the Executive Branch, while the Advocacy Department sits under the Legislative Branch's sphere and is overseen by the Chief Diversity Officer. The Executive Cabinet, as listed for 2025-26, consists of these offices: President, Vice President, Chief of Staff, Chief Financial Officer, Chief Communications Officer, Chief Programming Officer, Chief Diversity Officer, and Speaker of the Senate. The Legislative Branch comprises the Vice President, Chief Diversity Officer, Speaker of the Senate, twelve senators, six standing committees, and the advocacy liaisons, supported by a Parliamentary Secretary, Legislative Aides, and Senate Aides. The Judicial Branch is the USG Judicial Council, made up of a Chief Justice and four Associate Justices. USG publishes an organizational structure diagram on its About page covering departments and positions. Students looking for the current holders of these offices are directed to the Meet Our Team page rather than to the structure pages. USG's navigation groups these pages under About Us, with separate landing pages for each branch and department, plus Resources, Calendar, Press and News, and Contact Us sections.

title: USG Executive Branch
content: The USG Executive Branch is described as the overseeing body of the Undergraduate Student Government. It consists of the elected President, the Vice President, their Chief of Staff, and the Executive Cabinet, which oversees the functions of the different departments within USG. The Executive Branch also contains the USG Communications, Programming, and Funding departments. The Executive Cabinet offices listed for the 2025-26 academic year are: President, Vice President, Chief of Staff, Chief Financial Officer, Chief Communications Officer, Chief Programming Officer, Chief Diversity Officer, and Speaker of the Senate. The President and Vice President are elected positions; the Chief of Staff and the other cabinet roles are appointed or confirmed roles within the organization. The page directs students who want to know who currently holds each office, or who want to contact a specific officer, to USG's Meet Our Team page. Because the Executive Branch houses the Funding, Programming, and Communications departments, questions about applying for student organization funding, about USG-run events and assemblies, or about publicity support for a recognized student organization all ultimately route through Executive Branch departments rather than through the Senate.

title: USG Legislative Branch and project tracker
content: USG calls its Legislative Branch the center of advocacy. Its stated aim is to create an inclusive, intentional, and collaborative space where students find solutions to student problems by partnering with other organizations and administrative offices. The branch consists of the Vice President, the Chief Diversity Officer, the Speaker of the Senate, 12 senators, 6 standing committees, and the advocacy liaisons, with support from the Parliamentary Secretary, Legislative Aides, and Senate Aides. Together they represent undergraduate interests and seek middle-ground solutions among students, staff, faculty, and the community. The branch page links to three sub-areas: the Senate, the Standing Committees, and the Advocacy Department. It also hosts a public project tracker. The overview figures displayed on the page include 52 active projects, $19,000 total budget allocated, and 49,323 students impacted, alongside a second panel showing 34 active projects and $10,000 total budget allocated, with a next deadline of December 1. Listed projects and their status include: a LAX to USC return shuttle after winter break run by the Campus Infrastructure and Sustainability committee (two shuttle buses on January 11 and 12, hourly); a USC and LAFD fire-education workshop under External Affairs; Wellness Week II, a week-long event with RSOs on health and wellness topics; dining nutrition and allergen information added to the USC Dining app (completed); expanding study spaces for finals after library hours; a student housing accommodation request template; a disability awareness talk; OSAS and KCLC workshops; a move to Speechify for text-to-speech accommodations; priority seating on the first floor of Leavey Library for students with mobility needs; and a FAFSA guide and workshop.

title: USG Senate: composition, role, and legislation
content: The USG Senate consists of twelve elected senators who represent the interests of USC undergraduates. The Senate page encourages students who have an idea or project to improve USC to start with a senator, noting that senators are interested in partnering with students on both long-term projects and smaller campus changes. Senators are also presented as knowledgeable about campus resources and as advocates for campus organizations. A student organization that wants a senator to attend its meeting is told to contact the Speaker of the Senate at usgsots@usc.edu. The current body is identified as the 145th Senate. The Senate publishes a meeting tracker listing bills and resolutions with their bill number, date introduced, sponsoring senators, committees assigned, vote summary, and date passed, each linked to the full text. Examples from the 145th Senate's published list include a bill to approve legislative funding for additional lounge and rest areas for the Accessibility Committee (SB 145-15, passed 1/27/2026, 12-0), a bill to approve legislative funding for Wellness Week (SB 145-14, passed 1/27/2026, 12-0), a resolution supporting listing the Office of Sustainability as a support system in all academic syllabi (SR 145-13, passed 1/13/2026, 11-0-1), a bill amending the 2025-2026 fiscal budget (SB 145-12, 11/11/2025), a bill amending the USG Elections Code (SB 145-10, passed 10/21/2025, 10-2), and bills approving the 2025-26 department guidelines for Funding, Programming, Legislative, Communications, and the Allocations Committee. The page notes the displayed data is truncated and that full details are in the linked documents.

title: USG legislative standing committees and what each covers
content: USG's legislative standing committees exist to advocate for improvements in the student experience and to make sure the student voice is heard on campus, particularly on new campus initiatives and policies. There are six committees, each with published meeting agendas. Academic Affairs focuses on policies and programs affecting the academic experience and learning environment for undergraduates; past and current projects include the USC and QuASA Pronouns Pledge and adding a DEI question to course evaluations. Accessibility focuses on USC's compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 and on raising awareness of the needs of students with disabilities; projects include an ADA non-compliance form and an accessibility scavenger hunt. Affordability and Basic Needs focuses on students' financial barriers on campus, access to basic needs, and support for FGLI and undocumented student communities; projects include a meal swipe donation program and a work-study alternative for undocumented students. External Affairs focuses on the immediate USC surrounding community, USC's relationship with Los Angeles County and local government, and other outside organizations; projects include Fryft expansion and Counselors Not Cops. Sustainability and Campus Infrastructure focuses on infrastructure, safety, hospitality, and sustainable campus operations; projects include eliminating single-use plastics and adding recycling bins on the Row. Wellness Affairs focuses on advancing students' well-being and holistic health across sexual, mental, spiritual, and physical dimensions; projects include a wellness handbook and expanding naloxone access. Each committee description notes that its scope is not limited to the examples given.

title: USG Judicial Council and judicial codes
content: The USG Judicial Council is the Judicial Branch of the Undergraduate Student Government. It is made up of the Chief Justice and four Associate Justices. The Council interprets the USG Constitution and bylaws, reviews cases involving actions by other branches, and works to ensure that student government operates fairly and in line with its governing documents. It also oversees and enforces the policies that guide USG elections each year. Students with questions or concerns are directed to contact the Judicial Council at usgelect@usc.edu. The Council publishes three governing codes: the Elections Code, the Governing Document Violation Code, and the Personnel, Disciplinary and Impeachment Code. It also publishes three complaint forms that students can file: an Election Complaint Form, a Governing Document Violation Complaint Form, and a Personnel, Disciplinary and Impeachment Form. The Council publishes its written opinions by academic year, with sets posted for 2025-26, 2024-25, 2023-24, 2022-23, and 2018-19; case names are listed on the page with links to the full opinions. The Judicial Branch's stated values, as summarized on USG's About page, are integrity, professionalism, and transparency in all of USG's operations.

title: USG elections oversight, Elections Code, and complaints
content: USG does not maintain a separate public elections landing page; the publicly posted elections information lives on the Judicial Branch page. The USG Judicial Council oversees and enforces the policies that guide USG elections each year. The Council publishes the USG Elections Code as a public document, and students can file an Election Complaint Form, also linked from the same page. Election-related questions and concerns go to the Judicial Council at usgelect@usc.edu. The Elections Code is amended by legislation: the Senate's published meeting tracker records SB 145-10, a bill to amend the Undergraduate Student Government Elections Code, introduced 10/21/2025 and passed the same day by a 10-2 vote, authored by the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice Pro Tempore, and three Associate Justices. Judicial opinions arising from election disputes are published by academic year on the Judicial Branch page. Separately, USG's Executive Branch page notes that the President and Vice President are elected positions, and the Senate consists of twelve elected senators, so both the executive ticket and Senate seats are filled by undergraduate vote. Specific candidate filing deadlines, campaign periods, and voting dates for a given year are not published on these pages; students needing those dates would have to consult the Elections Code document or contact usgelect@usc.edu.

title: USG Funding Department and its four funds
content: The USG Funding Department supports student programs, ideas, and development, and asks applicants to work out their funding needs, review the relevant policies, and only then proceed to the application. The department states it can allocate up to $356,100 toward undergraduate students and recognized student organizations (RSOs) over the school year. There are four funds. The Professional and Academic Research Fund covers events programmed by recognized student organizations that educate and advance students' future professional careers, and academic research projects conducted by a USC undergraduate or by a group of USC students that is mostly undergraduates. The Philanthropy Fund covers community service projects sponsored by recognized student organizations. The Social and Recreation/Startup Fund covers events programmed by RSOs to celebrate, highlight, or foster a sense of community for the student group, and also supports student organizations first registered with the Office of Campus Activities within the last two academic semesters (fall or spring) for promotion and membership recruitment. The Performing and Visual Arts Fund covers events programmed by RSOs to celebrate, highlight, or foster a sense of community. The application form is for recognized student organizations and USC undergraduate students requesting funds from the department, and is accessed through EngageSC (login required); a sample application is published for reference. The department publishes an application breakdown presentation explaining what each board can and cannot fund, plus the full funding guidelines. The page notes that as of September 28, 2026 it lists the estimated remaining funding in the department, and links an FY26 Funding Department Financial Report. Questions go to usgfunds@usc.edu, and the department states that organizations and individuals who ask questions are more successful in the funding process than those who do not.

title: USG funding deadlines, limits, and FAQ
content: Deadlines: USG funding applications must be submitted on Wednesdays by 11:59 PM, six academic weeks before the event date when using an approved vendor, and/or nine academic weeks before the initial payment due date, whichever comes first, for approved USC vendors. The Funding Department publishes an application timeline graphic described as a nine-week timeline. Limits: each RSO can have up to four events funded per semester, as long as the organization stays under $8,000 from the USG Funding Department per year. How to apply: review the Funding Guidelines and complete the Funding Guidelines modules during the RSO Recognition process; the application itself is accessed through EngageSC. USG Funding processes payments on the organization's behalf rather than reimbursing the organization directly. Funding is not guaranteed; the department states that awards depend on various factors and recommends submitting applications early and exploring other funding sources across USC. Other sources USG names for student organizations are fundraising, crowdfunding through IgniteSC, membership fees, USC academic departments, USC grants, fellowships or scholarships, USG programming assemblies and committees, partnering with other RSOs, and donations from donors or USC alumni; the department links a document listing other funding sources. A sample funding application and an exhaustive FAQ document are both published. Application-specific questions go to usgfunds@usc.edu.

title: USG Programming Department and its 16 assemblies
content: The USG Programming Department works formally with campus student organizations to coordinate activities and pool resources. It is made up of special interest committees and community-focused assemblies with the shared goal of promoting diversity, education, and entertainment through on-campus events. For 2025-26 the Programming Branch lists 16 community-focused assemblies that represent students from a wide variety of backgrounds. Assemblies act as umbrella organizations for member organizations, which take part in event planning and information sharing at assembly meetings, and assemblies also serve as a source of funding and advisement for their member organizations. The 16 assemblies are: Academic Culture Assembly (usgaca@usc.edu), Asian Pacific American Student Assembly (apasa@usc.edu), Black Student Assembly (usgbsa@usc.edu), Environmental Student Assembly (uscesa@usc.edu), First Generation Student Assembly, International Student Assembly (usgisa@usc.edu), Joint Assembly for Military-Associated Students (usgjams@usc.edu), Latine Student Assembly (usglsa@usc.edu), Native American Student Assembly (uscnasa@usc.edu), Middle Eastern North African Student Assembly, Political Student Assembly (uscpsa@usc.edu), Queer and Ally Student Assembly (quasa@usc.edu), Student Assembly for Accessibility, Student Assembly for Gender Empowerment (uscsage@usc.edu), Transfer Student Assembly (tsausc@usc.edu), and Immigrant Trojan Student Assembly (usgutsa@usc.edu), which supports undocumented-plus students and allies and defines undocumented-plus as including undocumented, DACAmented, TPS, refugee, asylum-seeker, U-visa, and students pursuing legalization. The International Student Assembly works closely with USG, its member organizations, and the Office of International Services, and serves as the umbrella for most nationality clubs on campus. QuASA's recurring events include an annual Drag Show, Second Chance Prom, National Coming Out Month, and leadership retreats. The assembly list is noted as last updated 10/22/26.

title: USG programming committees: concerts, performing arts, speakers, spirit
content: Alongside its assemblies, the USG Programming Department runs four special-interest committees for 2025-26, focused on concerts, performing arts, guest speakers, and school spirit. The Concerts Committee organizes concerts and programs to bring bands and musicians to campus, and also hosts entertainment-industry figures for a speaker series giving members insight into working in the music industry. Anyone interested in live music is invited to its meetings on Mondays at 9:00 pm in TCC 450; contact sconcert@usc.edu. The Performing Arts Committee creates opportunities for students interested in visual and performing arts, fostering collaboration among USC artists and bringing in outside performers across dance, music, theater, painting, and photography; contact usgpac@usc.edu. Trojan Pride is the spirit group that coordinates with the athletic department to increase visibility and attendance at USC athletic events, including home football and basketball games and away games across the state; contact scpride@usc.edu. The Speakers Committee brings a range of speakers to campus each year for insight, education, entertainment, and cultural awareness; past speakers listed include Barack Obama, Maya Angelou, Stan Lee, and Angela Davis, and the committee states that all are welcome to join; contact speakers@usc.edu. Each committee and assembly lists an official Instagram account on the Programming page for students who want to follow its events.

title: USG Advocacy Department and advocacy liaisons
content: The USG Advocacy Department works to advance community-centered advocacy by bridging the gap between university administrators and students on issues affecting campus communities. Its stated goals are to keep students informed about important institutional changes and to increase awareness of campus resources and support, and to ensure the voices and lived experiences of the undergraduate student body are actively represented to university administrators through strong partnerships. The department operates under the oversight of the Chief Diversity Officer. It is made up of Advocacy Liaisons, who serve as stewards of advocacy priorities, initiatives, and projects for various community groups on campus. Liaisons are nominated by student assemblies and campus offices, and they represent their communities in work with key administrators, staff, and faculty to create solutions that reflect the needs and interests of students and the wider university community. For 2025-26, advocacy liaison positions are listed for the Asian Pacific American Student Assembly, Black Student Assembly, Environmental Student Assembly, First Generation Student Assembly, International Student Assembly, Joint Assembly for Military-Associated Students, Latine Student Assembly, Middle Eastern North African Student Assembly, Native American Student Assembly, Queer and Ally Student Assembly, Student Assembly for Accessibility, Student Assembly for Gender Empowerment, Transfer Student Assembly, and Immigrant Trojan Student Assembly. The USC Office of Religious and Spiritual Life has two liaison seats: a Muslim Community Advocacy Liaison and a Jewish Community Advocacy Liaison.

title: USG Communications Department and promotion support for student orgs
content: The USG Communications Department is the primary liaison between USG, the student body, media, and other third parties. Its members work to create transparency within USG, to communicate USG's projects, events, and initiatives, and to increase student engagement by promoting student organizations and communities across the university. Its three stated mission priorities are to create more evergreen content explaining USG and USC resources, to grow its audience through more promotional content and revitalized social media, and to increase campus collaboration. The department has four teams. Creative Services oversees all aspects of graphic design, has approval over all graphics used by the organization, and produces event graphics, infographics, motion graphics, and promotional items. Digital Strategy leads marketing outreach, spearheads promotional campaigns, sets social media strategy, oversees communication of USG's informational resources, and works with Programming committees and assemblies to market USG at events. Media handles photography and videography for USG's promotional needs, working with Digital Strategy to document the organization's work and events. Public Relations manages relationships and partnerships with external entities including student media, registered student organizations, staff, faculty, and the student body, and drafts public statements, press releases, community letters, and memorandums relating to USG or its subsidiary bodies. Students and RSOs needing an advertisement for social media, a newsletter feature, a graphic for an event, or a photographer or videographer are directed to submit the department's content form; the form is also the route for graphics, headshots, and event coverage. For promotional needs such as Instagram story reposts, the department asks groups to direct message its official account, @uscusg.

title: Joining USG: recruitment cycle and where applications are posted
content: USG runs recruitment cycles for positions within the organization and posts them on its Get Involved page. As published, applications for the Fall 2026 recruitment cycle are now closed, and the page directs students to follow the official USG Instagram account (@uscusg) for updates about future application cycles. For students deciding where in the organization they might fit, the page links to USG's structure and branches overview and displays the organizational structure chart. Beyond formal recruitment, USG's other pages describe several standing ways to take part that do not require an application cycle. The Senate meets weekly and attendees are welcome to voice concerns during open forum. The six legislative standing committees hold their own meetings, listed as Academic Affairs, Accessibility, Affordability and Basic Needs, External Affairs, Sustainability and Campus Infrastructures, and Wellness Affairs, and the Legislative Branch page invites students to come to one of them. Programming committees such as Concerts (Mondays at 9:00 pm in TCC 450) and the Speakers Committee state that interested students are welcome at their meetings. Programming assemblies act as umbrella organizations whose member organizations participate in assembly meetings. Students with a project idea are encouraged to contact a senator, and organizations that want a senator at their meeting can contact the Speaker of the Senate at usgsots@usc.edu.

title: USG Senate meetings: when, where, and how to attend
content: USG Senate meetings are open to students. The Legislative Branch page states that the Senate meets every Tuesday at 7pm in TCC 450, which is a room in the Ronald Tutor Campus Center. USG's homepage adds that the Senate meets in person every week to discuss current projects and ongoing policy implementation, that attendees are welcome to voice their concerns during open forum, and that students who cannot attend in person can join online on Tuesdays through a published USC Zoom link. Agendas and past meeting minutes are posted in a public Google Drive folder linked from both the homepage and the Legislative Branch page. Beyond the Senate itself, the six legislative standing committees hold their own meetings and publish meeting agendas in separate public Drive folders, one per committee. USG also maintains a main calendar covering Senate meetings and programming events, and a published office hours and staff roster spreadsheet; the homepage describes the office hours sheet as the place to check when USG members are available. Individual programming committees list their own meeting times, for example the Concerts Committee on Mondays at 9:00 pm in TCC 450. For GSG-style appointment scheduling USG instead directs students to its Meet Our Team page to contact specific officers.

title: How to contact USG: office, email, and feedback form
content: USG's office is at 3607 Trousdale Parkway, SKS 404, Los Angeles, CA 90089. The Contact Us page states that students can reach USG by submitting the online form or by emailing usg@usc.edu, and directs anyone trying to reach a specific officer to the Meet Our Team page. The contact page hosts a Qualtrics-based USG Student Feedback and Concerns form, described as a way for students to anonymously share concerns, ideas, or questions with campus leaders; the page frames USG's role as listening and advocating for students. USG's site footer repeats the mailing address and the usg@usc.edu address, and notes that the site is designed and operated by the Undergraduate Student Government, with website issues directed to USC Provost IT. Other published official channels for specific needs: usgfunds@usc.edu for funding applications and questions, usgsots@usc.edu for the Speaker of the Senate and requests to have a senator attend a student organization meeting, usgelect@usc.edu for the Judicial Council and election matters, and usgvp@usc.edu and usgcdo@usc.edu for the Vice President and Chief Diversity Officer. USG also runs a newsletter with a public Qualtrics subscription form, a Communications content request form for graphics and event coverage, and the Instagram account @uscusg. Official social links published on USG's pages include its Instagram account; a Facebook page for USC Undergraduate Student Government and a LinkedIn company page also exist but are not linked from the site pages collected here.

title: USG governing documents, budget, and office hours
content: USG publishes its governing documents on its Resources page, described as containing information about the role of departments, directors, elected representatives, and the organization as a whole. The documents named there are the Constitution, the Bylaws, and the Code of Ethics. A second section on the same page offers additional documents: a Policies Manual, the Office Hours listing, and a budget labeled Budget FY24-25. The page also links a free USC resources section and an LA Transit Guide, and notes it was updated 03/05/26. USG's site footer separately links the Constitution and the Bylaws as Google Docs, along with an Office Hours and Staff Roster spreadsheet and USG Brand Guidelines. The Judicial Council publishes three further governing codes that sit under the Constitution and bylaws: the Elections Code, the Governing Document Violation Code, and the Personnel, Disciplinary and Impeachment Code, each as a public document, together with the corresponding complaint forms. Governing documents are amended through the Senate: the Senate meeting tracker records bills approving the annual Senate Meeting Rules, the Office Policy Manual, the 2025-26 department guidelines for Funding, Programming, Legislative, Communications, and the Allocations Committee, and an amendment to the Elections Code. An older copy of the USG Bylaws dated April 2020 is also hosted on the usg.usc.edu site as a PDF.

title: USG financial support and basic needs resource list
content: USG's Financial Support resources page curates links to USC and Los Angeles programs for students facing housing, food, or financial insecurity. It does not describe USG-run programs so much as point students to existing services. The resources listed are: USC Housing Support Resources through the Student Basic Needs office; Legal Counseling Services, accessed through a Google Form; the Coalition for Economic Survival Tenant's Rights Legal Clinic; TRiO Programs through USC Educational Partnerships; Financial Insecurity Resources, listed as economic support through Student Basic Needs; Academic and International Fellowships through the USC Academic Honors and Fellowships office; a Stay Housed LA referral; Los Angeles Housing Authority resources through housing.lacity.gov; the USC Basic Needs Resource Guide; the Norman Topping Student Aid Fund; and the Trojan Food Pantry, also run through Student Basic Needs. The page is part of USG's broader Resources section, which also covers emergency contacts, advocacy and academic support, health and wellness support, and getting involved. The page notes it was updated 03/05/26. Students who want something added to USG's resource pages are asked to contact a USG member, and the related guides page specifies the Communications Department's Digital Strategy Team for corrections or recommendations.

title: USG academic support and advocacy center directory
content: USG's Advocacy and Academic Support page is a directory connecting students to resources inside and outside USC. It has two parts. The first, Academic Resource Guides, groups links under Support and Intervention, Career Center, International Students, and Undocumented Students. The second lists recognized campus organizations and centers that provide additional services, from legal assistance to culturally relevant programming, each with a phone number, a shared office email where available, and an office location. The centers listed are: Academic Honors and Fellowships, (213) 740-9116, ahfstaff@usc.edu, STU 300; Asian Pacific American Student Services, (213) 740-4999, apass@usc.edu, STU 410; Center for Black Cultural and Student Affairs, (213) 740-8257, cbcsa@usc.edu, STU 415; Center for Engineering Diversity, (213) 740-1999, RTH 210; Center for the Study of Immigration Integration, (213) 740-3643, csii@usc.edu, JEF 102; Kortschak Center for Learning and Creativity, (213) 740-7884, kortschakcenter@usc.edu, STU 311; La Casa, (213) 740-1480, ecc@usc.edu, STU 402; Latino Forum, (213) 821-5363; LGBT Resource Center, (213) 740-7619, lgbt@usc.edu, STU 202B; Norman Topping Student Aid Fund, (213) 740-7575, ntsaf@usc.edu, RTCC 425; Relationship and Sexual Violence Prevention and Services, (213) 740-4900, ESH 356; Tomas Rivera Policy Institute, (213) 821-5615, PPD 201; TRiO Programs, (213) 821-2402, RAN 262; and the Writing Center, (213) 740-3691, THH 321. The page is marked updated 03/05/26 and carries a notice that it is being reviewed for pending updates, with recommendations or concerns directed to the Communications Department's Digital Strategy Team.

title: USG health and wellness support resources
content: USG's Health and Wellness Support page gathers links for student health and mental health needs. Its top section links resources for HIV testing, RSVP services (USC's Relationship and Sexual Violence Prevention and Services), Student Health, and a menstrual product map. Its Counseling and Mental Health section lists three resources with short descriptions. USC Student Mental Health and Counseling is presented through the USC Student Health portal, where students can learn about individual and group therapy, crisis support, psychiatric services, and specialties for gender-based harm. Crisis Text Line is described as a free service connecting individuals in any type of crisis to a trained crisis counselor, with more information and resources on its website. The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is described as a national network of local crisis centers providing free and confidential emotional support to people in suicidal crisis or emotional distress, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, in the United States. The page is one of five sections in USG's Resources area, alongside emergency contacts, financial support, advocacy and academic support, and get involved. It notes it was updated 03/05/26. USG's Wellness Affairs standing committee, which focuses on sexual, mental, spiritual, and physical health, is the legislative counterpart to this resource list, and GSG separately publishes a USG Official Wellness Resource Guide PDF on its own student resources page.

title: What GSG is, its mission, and who it represents
content: USC Graduate Student Government (GSG) is a student-led organization that represents the 27,500-plus graduate and professional students at USC. Its stated mission is to enhance the USC graduate and professional student experience by serving as the face of the student body, and a second mission statement on the same page frames this as amplifying student voices and working with USC administrators and senior leadership. To do that, GSG says it manages student resources efficiently, provides a voice for the student community, builds a community that fosters interdisciplinary exchanges, and informs students about their rights, resources, and opportunities. Summarizing what it does, GSG states that it advocates for student needs, manages student resources, and fosters an interdisciplinary community through programmed events. The work is carried out by elected officers, senators who represent all schools and departments, and special interest committees that tackle issues specific to graduate and professional students and create venues for interaction beyond the academic realm. Students also participate in GSG and university committees, meet with administration and faculty on issues of joint importance, and draw on the expertise of administration professionals who serve students. GSG describes itself as working continuously and closely with university officials to enhance graduate and professional student life, and says these close ties let it better meet student needs. Its site sections cover About (Executive Board, GSG Senate, Committees), Resources (RSO funding, accessibility, student resources, DACA resources, COVID-19 resources, publicity and branding), Communications and Events (resolutions, USC events), its EngageSC community, and food resources.

title: GSG structure: Executive Board, Senate, and committees
content: GSG has three moving parts: an Executive Board, a Senate, and committees. The Executive Board consists of 29 officers selected every spring by the GSG senators together with the outgoing executive board members. The Board oversees the daily operations of GSG and works closely with the Senate to promote graduate and professional student interests within the USC administration and academic departments; the homepage posts the Executive Board for 2026-2027. GSG senators are elected by their peers in their particular academic department or school and meet monthly to address issues and concerns of the graduate and professional student population. The Senate's committees are made up of student volunteers, with committee chairs elected within the committees, and they provide GSG with special interest programming as well as the research and recommendations behind its advocacy initiatives. Organizationally the Executive Board is divided into three branches, as published on the Executive Board page: an Administration Branch, an Advocacy Branch, and a Programming Branch, each led by a Vice President, with the President and Senior Vice President above them. The homepage notes that meetings with Executive Board members are by appointment and that students should reach out directly to schedule a time; many officers publish a scheduling link. Because officers are selected by senators and senators are elected within each school, a graduate student's most direct route into GSG decision-making is the senator for their own academic unit.

title: GSG Executive Board offices and their role emails
content: GSG publishes its Executive Board as a table of office titles with a shared GSG role email for each. The two top offices are President (gsgpres@usc.edu) and Senior Vice President (gsgsvp@usc.edu). The Administration Branch is led by the Vice President of Administration (gsgvpadm@usc.edu) and includes the Director of Governance and Senate Affairs (gsggov@usc.edu), the Chief of Staff (gsgchst@usc.edu), and five finance and grants roles: Director of Finance - Internal Approvals (gsgfinia@usc.edu), Director of Finance - Operations (gsgfinop@usc.edu), Director of Finance - Approvals (gsgfinap@usc.edu), Director of Finance - Strategy (gsgfinst@usc.edu), and Director of Grants (gsgtgea@usc.edu). The Advocacy Branch is led by the Vice President of Advocacy (gsgvpadv@usc.edu) and includes the Director of Accessibility Affairs (gsgaxaf@usc.edu), Director of Campus Affairs (gsgcamp@usc.edu), Director of Student Belonging - Advocacy (gsgdiv@usc.edu), Director of External Affairs (gsgexaf@usc.edu), Director of Globalization and Inclusion (gsggi@usc.edu), Director of Sustainability (gsgsust@usc.edu), Director of Virtual Accessibility (gsgvrax@usc.edu), and an HSC Director of Student Belonging (gsghscde@usc.edu). The Programming Branch is led by the Vice President of Programming (gsgvppro@usc.edu) and includes the Director of Academic Affairs (gsgacad@usc.edu), Director of Communications (gsgcomm@usc.edu), Director of Community Service (gsgcs@usc.edu), Director of Student Belonging - Programming (gsgsbpro@usc.edu), Director of Social Programming (gsgsoc@usc.edu), an HSC Director of Community Service (gsghsccs@usc.edu), and the Director of Engagement and Recruitment (gsger@usc.edu). These are role-based addresses that carry over between officeholders, so they are the durable way to reach a GSG portfolio.

title: GSG Senate: role, powers, and which units have senators
content: GSG senators are central to the organization because, as the Senate page puts it, Senate approval is required to effect change. Their listed responsibilities include carrying out committee goals, electing the GSG President and Senior Vice President, confirming Vice President and Director positions, and approving the GSG budget. Senators are elected to represent the recognized student organization of an academic unit and are expected to dedicate 10 hours per semester to senator responsibilities. GSG strongly recommends that graduate students reach out to their own senator with any questions or concerns about GSG, describing the senator as a direct bridge between the student body and GSG. Senate meetings are open to all; the page directs students to EngageSC for registration information. The published contact table maps each school or academic unit to the student organization whose senator represents it, covering the Keck School of Medicine (including the Master of Public Health Student Association, Associated Students of the School of Medicine, School of Medicine Graduate Student Association, and Physician Assistant Student Association), Ostrow School of Dentistry, Annenberg, the Chan Division of Occupational Science and Occupational Therapy, Davis School of Gerontology, Biokinesiology and Physical Therapy, Dornsife (with separate humanities, natural sciences, and social sciences seats), Dworak-Peck School of Social Work, Gould School of Law, Leventhal School of Accounting, Mann School of Pharmacy, Marshall School of Business, Price School of Public Policy, Roski School of Art and Design, Rossier School of Education, School of Architecture, School of Cinematic Arts, School of Dramatic Arts, Thornton School of Music, and Viterbi School of Engineering. The table also publishes each organization's shared RSO email, and marks seats that are vacant, filled by a proxy, or represented by an academic unit contact.

title: GSG standing committees and volunteer commitments
content: GSG's standing committees are permanent committees needed to run essential aspects of GSG. As published for the 2025-2026 academic year, there are four. The Finance Committee reviews and processes all funding applications submitted to GSG, checks that applications comply with GSG funding policies, evaluates each request's impact on graduate students, and gives feedback on finance policies and procedures and input on the GSG budget; its stated goals are weekly review of RSO funding applications, auditing approved and funded events at the committee's discretion, and suggesting improvements to the funding process. Expected volunteer commitment is about 10-12 hours per semester for the full academic year, and it is led by the Director of Finance - Approvals (gsgupcfi@usc.edu) and the HSC Director of Finance (gsghscfi@usc.edu). The Health Sciences Campus Research and Development Committee serves HSC student interests, advises GSG on HSC matters, assists with HSC-wide social and volunteer events, and develops diversity programming; at least one HSC senator from an HSC student organization must be present, and a proxy may attend in their place. Its goals include bringing equitable university resources to HSC, such as the Campus Activities office and resource centers, and relaying HSC-specific concerns at monthly meetings; the commitment is monthly one-hour meetings plus at least one HSC event, and it is led by the Senior Vice President (gsgsvp@usc.edu). The Grants Review Committee reviews hundreds of applications each Fall and Spring for Emergency Fund, Caretaker Subsidy, and Neuropsych grant eligibility, mostly remotely, at roughly 5-10 hours per semester, led by the Director of Grants (gsgtgea@usc.edu). The Presidential Strategy and Innovation Committee acts as a quality-control body and think tank, reviewing GSG initiatives, policies, and operations and incubating longer-term projects, and may convene special task forces on emergency response, external partnerships, and sustainability and futures; commitment is about 8-10 hours per semester, led by the President (gsgpres@usc.edu). The page links a public form for students who want to join a committee.

title: GSG funding for recognized student organizations
content: GSG funding opportunities for recognized student organizations support graduate student-run programming related to cultural, academic, and social enrichment. The money comes from the Student Programming Fee that all graduate students pay into, and in that spirit GSG General Funds are distributed to support RSO events. Applying is a four-step process, and GSG stresses doing the training early because applications are due 6-8 weeks before the event date, with the exact lead time varying by event type. Step one is completing the mandatory GSG Finance training: review the online orientation, then take the assessment whose link appears at the end of the presentation. Step two is passing the Finance Assessment, which demonstrates understanding of application requirements and responsibilities and is mandatory to be able to open the application at all. Step three is referencing the RSO Funding Guidebook and the other published resources to review detailed requirements before applying. Step four is submitting the application on GSG's EngageSC page. A designated representative from the organization, for example the treasurer, must complete the mandatory training to access the application. GSG publishes a set of 2026-27 links for all of this: the RSO Funding Guidebook, the GSG Finance Orientation video, the Finance Assessment, the funding application on EngageSC, and a calendar of submission deadlines. Supporting application materials include an approved vendor list, an event flyer template, a Constituency Organization Approval Memo, a transportation waiver form, and a prize recipient form. GSG also runs a Finance Newsletter with a public subscription link for funding updates.

title: GSG Professional Development Fund Program and Graduate Research Symposium
content: The GSG Professional Development Fund Program aims to support USC graduate and professional students in activities related to developing the skills needed for success after graduation. All students who have paid the Graduate Student Programming Fee are eligible to apply. The program consists of two awards: the GSG Travel Award and the GSG Empowerment Award, each with its own application page on GSG's EngageSC site. The program is run by GSG's Academic Affairs portfolio; questions go to the Director of Academic Affairs at gsgacad@usc.edu and the Director of Grants at gsgtgea@usc.edu. GSG Academic Affairs also runs the Graduate Research Symposium, described as a platform for USC graduate students from all disciplines to exhibit their research. The symposium program includes keynote speakers, panel discussions, research presentations, and interactive poster sessions, and GSG frames it as a chance to expand a professional network, refine academic skills, take part in peer-to-peer learning, and potentially win awards for scholarly contributions. A separate symposium page carries the details. Beyond these, GSG's Grants Review Committee handles applications for three other grant programs named on its committees page: an Emergency Fund, a Caretaker Subsidy, and a Neuropsychological Evaluation Fund, reviewed during the Fall and Spring semesters. Applications for all GSG grant programs run through the GSG organization on EngageSC, which students must join before applying for the first time.

title: GSG Travel Award: amount, cycle, and eligibility
content: The GSG Travel Award is part of the GSG Professional Development Fund Program and is designed as a last-resort source of funding for students who could not obtain funding elsewhere, such as from their program, advisor, conference or workshop organizers, fellowships, or scholarships, or whose other funding does not cover their full expenses. The funding limit is $500 per student per academic year, with the current academic year given as August 2026 to May 2027. The application cycle is open September 9-30, and applications are submitted through EngageSC; all applicants must be members of the GSG EngageSC community to access the form. Eligibility: the applicant must be a registered USC graduate student both at the time of the request and at the time of award disbursement, and must have paid the Graduate Student Programming Fee for the semester in which they apply. Post-doctoral fellows and undergraduates are not eligible unless they can prove payment of the Graduate Student Programming Fee. Enrollment is required to receive disbursement, and students working on a dissertation must still be enrolled in a non-enrollment course. Students may receive a maximum of one award per academic year and may submit at most one application per semester. Requests may cover an anticipated expense, justified by official vendor quotes, or a past expense contributing to a future conference if it occurred, or the receipt is dated, within the last six months of submission, documented by receipts. Qualifying expenses include travel or registration fees for academic or professional conferences, professional organization membership fees for travel discounts, conference accommodation, conference transportation, and abstract submission fees. The award may not be used for tuition or fees associated with enrollment in a USC degree program. GSG notes that PhD students should look first to department, grant, or fellowship funding, and that faculty and staff should not direct doctoral students to this fund as a first resort.

title: GSG Travel Award application process and what to expect
content: Applications for the GSG Travel Award may be submitted any time during the open application period and are reviewed during the current semester by a committee of two or more graduate students, through GSG's online portal. First-time applicants to any GSG grant program, which includes the Travel Award, Empowerment Award, Caretaker Subsidy, Emergency Fund, and Neuropsychological Evaluation Fund, must first join the GSG organization on EngageSC. All materials must be in English and uploaded as PDFs. Required items are a personal statement that clearly states the conference name, time frame, and location; a signature page on which the faculty advisor, or the department academic advisor if the faculty advisor is unavailable, verifies whether alternative funding is available, with documentation of any alternative funding attached; and funding details, meaning a budget of anticipated costs plus quotes, invoices, estimates, or screenshots supporting the amounts, clearly stating the total requested. Vendor quotes must be legible and show the total amount, expected dates of service, and the vendor name. Multiple receipts must be combined into one PDF, and missing, incomplete, illegible, or corrupt documents delay review. What to expect: an application may be selected for an award, returned with changes needed for eligibility, or rejected. The Director of Academic Affairs may message applicants through the portal or by email at gsgacad@usc.edu to request more information. Approved applicants can expect to receive the award by the end of the academic semester, and international students should anticipate up to three months. Most awards are paid as a single lump-sum grant, processed as stipends, which may affect financial aid packages; all applications are reviewed by the Office of Financial Aid as part of disbursement, and students whose aid would be adversely affected are advised to work with that office before accepting. International students living outside the United States may owe taxes on the award. The award is not guaranteed and depends on fund availability, and applicants should wait 8-10 weeks after the deadline closes before following up. GSG reviews applications only; award processing is administered by USC Campus Activities, and the program is funded through the Graduate Student Programming Fee.

title: GSG Constitution and Bylaws
content: GSG publishes its two governing documents directly on its homepage under the heading Constitution and Bylaws: the GSG Constitution, labeled as updated January 2024, and the GSG Bylaws, also labeled as updated January 2024. Both are posted as public Google Docs. These documents are the authority for how GSG is organized and how its officers are chosen, and the structural facts GSG states elsewhere on its site follow from them: an Executive Board of 29 officers selected every spring by the GSG senators and the outgoing executive board members; senators elected by their peers within each academic department or school; Senate approval required to effect change, including electing the President and Senior Vice President, confirming Vice President and Director positions, and approving the GSG budget; and committees made up of student volunteers whose chairs are elected within the committees. Because both documents carry a January 2024 revision date, a student researching current GSG procedure should treat them as the most recent published version while noting that the posted date is from the 2023-24 academic year. GSG separately publishes resolutions passed by its Senate, a publicity and branding page, and, for the funding process, an RSO Funding Guidebook, all of which sit beneath the Constitution and Bylaws in authority.

title: GSG offices, hours, and official channels
content: GSG lists two offices in the footer of every page on its site. The main campus (UPC) office, noted as a new location, is at 3607 Trousdale Pkwy, SKS 410, Los Angeles, CA 90089, with business hours Monday to Friday, 9:00 am to 5:00 pm. The Health Sciences Campus (HSC) office is at 1969 Zonal Avenue, described as next to Starbucks, Los Angeles, CA 90033, with business hours Monday to Friday, 12:00 pm to 5:00 pm. Rather than a single general inbox, GSG publishes a role-based email for each Executive Board office, for example gsgpres@usc.edu for the President, gsgsvp@usc.edu for the Senior Vice President, gsggov@usc.edu for the Director of Governance and Senate Affairs, gsgacad@usc.edu for the Director of Academic Affairs, gsgcomm@usc.edu for the Director of Communications, and gsgaxaf@usc.edu for the Director of Accessibility Affairs. Meetings with Executive Board members are by appointment, and students are asked to reach out directly to schedule; many officers publish a personal scheduling link next to their listing. For most student questions GSG recommends contacting the senator for your own school or academic unit first, and the Senate page publishes each academic unit's organization email. GSG's official social links, published in its site header, are Facebook at facebook.com/uscgsg, Twitter/X at twitter.com/uscgsg, and Instagram at instagram.com/uscgsg. GSG also maintains a community on USC's EngageSC platform, which is where committee sign-ups, Senate meeting registration, funding applications, and grant applications are handled. The site is run under the USC Office of the Provost.

title: How GSG officers and senators are chosen
content: GSG's published pages describe a two-tier selection process rather than a campus-wide general election for every office. Senators are elected by their peers in their particular academic department or school, and each senator is elected to represent the recognized student organization of an academic unit. Executive officers are then chosen by those senators: the homepage states that an Executive Board of 29 officers is selected every spring by the GSG senators together with the outgoing executive board members, and the Senate page lists electing the GSG President and Senior Vice President and confirming Vice President and Director positions among senators' core responsibilities. In other words, graduate students influence GSG leadership chiefly by electing their school's senator, and the senators in turn elect the President and Senior Vice President and confirm the rest of the board. The Executive Board posted on the homepage is labeled for 2026-2027, consistent with a spring selection cycle for the following academic year. GSG's Senate page notes that senator seats can be vacant, filled by a proxy, or represented by an academic unit contact, and it marks which units fall into each category, so a graduate student whose unit has no sitting senator can see that on the published table. Specific nomination deadlines, candidate requirements, and voting procedures are not published on GSG's public pages; those would be set out in the GSG Constitution and Bylaws, both posted as updated January 2024, or available from the Director of Governance and Senate Affairs at gsggov@usc.edu.

title: GSG student resources hub
content: GSG maintains a Student Resources hub that points graduate students to USC services and to GSG's own guides. It publishes two downloadable guides at the top: a Campus Partner Resources guide, also called the Campus Resource Guide, as a PDF dated to Fall 2023, and a Student Wellness Resource Guide PDF, which is the USG Official Wellness Resource Guide. The hub is then organized into sub-pages for General resources, Reporting, Student Life, and Student Health. It links several USC offices with short descriptions: the USC Office of Campus Wellbeing and Education, which works to develop a culture of wellbeing so that faculty, staff, and students have the tools, resources, guidance, and support to thrive; the Trojan Food Pantry, available to any currently enrolled USC student experiencing a food emergency or food insecurity; the Trojan Neighborhood Association, which brings together students and the community living within the USC DPS zone to address shared neighborhood problems; and the USC Department of Public Safety, described as one of the largest campus public safety departments in the United States, employing 306 full-time personnel and 30 part-time student workers. Under emergency resources it links a GSG wildfire resources document and a USC and Los Angeles food resources page. Under health and wellness it links a Preventing Harmful Environments resource guide, a guide to navigating student health insurance, and a list of USC buildings that provide free menstrual products, updated January 2025. Under GSG general resources it links a centralized spreadsheet of USC graduate scholarships, a student parent resources page, and recorded seminar resources. A GSG grants link points to the GSG organization on EngageSC.

title: Free goods and services GSG provides to graduate students
content: GSG lists a set of free goods and services for graduate students on its Student Resources page. GSG offers free New York Times subscriptions to students through a sign-up form, and separately offers free New York Times Games subscriptions through their own sign-up link. Free HIV testing is provided on campus by USC Student Health at both the Engemann and Eric Cohen student health centers and is available to undergraduate and graduate students. Legal services are run jointly: each year GSG and USG provide free legal counseling to the student population at USC, with legal counseling every Monday from 4:00 to 9:00 pm and each appointment lasting 30 minutes, booked through a published form. GSG also directs students to the Trojan Food Pantry for food emergencies and food insecurity, open to any currently enrolled USC student, and publishes a list of USC buildings that provide free menstrual products, updated January 2025. On the funding side, GSG's grant programs for individual students, administered through EngageSC, include the GSG Travel Award and GSG Empowerment Award under the Professional Development Fund Program, plus an Emergency Fund, a Caretaker Subsidy, and a Neuropsychological Evaluation Fund reviewed by the Grants Review Committee. Note that some sign-up links on the page may point to forms that have since closed for the year, including the legal counseling form, so students should check the current status before relying on a link.

title: GSG accessibility resources and where to raise concerns
content: GSG's accessibility page routes students to the right office depending on the kind of accessibility issue. For education-related accessibility issues, students are directed to OSAS, USC's Office of Student Accessibility Services. For institutional accessibility issues, students are directed to USC's ADA office at accessibility.usc.edu, which also has a report-a-concern form. The page highlights Disabled Access to Road Transportation (DART), a free service at the University Park Campus provided by USC Transportation during the Fall and Spring semesters, between 8:30 am and 6:00 pm, to assist Trojans with temporary mobility issues. GSG also recommends connecting with the Student Assembly for Accessibility, which it describes as an RSO that seeks to empower and represent students with a range of disabilities. Within GSG itself, there is a Director of Accessibility who students can contact at any time with questions or if they want someone to talk to, at gsgaxaf@usc.edu, and GSG has established an Accessibility Committee aimed at improving conditions for students facing accessibility-related issues. GSG's Executive Board also includes a Director of Virtual Accessibility at gsgvrax@usc.edu, covering accessibility of online and remote participation. Note that USG runs a parallel Accessibility standing committee on the undergraduate side, focused on USC's compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, so the two governments have separate accessibility tracks.

title: GSG food resources guide
content: GSG maintains a dedicated Food Resources page for graduate students. The page's main content is a downloadable Food Resource Guide, published as a Google Drive file, plus a series of graphics titled USC On-Campus Food Resources that summarize where students can find food support on campus. The page was last updated in late October 2025, and the graphics are dated to the same period. GSG links this page from its broader Student Resources hub under emergency resources, where it is labeled USC and Los Angeles Food Resources, indicating that the guide covers both on-campus and wider Los Angeles options. The related service GSG names elsewhere is the Trojan Food Pantry, available to any currently enrolled USC student experiencing a food emergency or food insecurity. Because the substance of the guide sits inside a downloadable file and image graphics rather than in page text, students needing specific pantry hours, locations, or eligibility rules should open the linked Food Resource Guide itself. On the undergraduate side, USG's Affordability and Basic Needs standing committee runs related work including a meal swipe donation program, and USG's financial support page links the Trojan Food Pantry and USC's Student Basic Needs food support resources.

title: Resolutions passed by the GSG Senate
content: GSG publishes the full archive of resolutions passed by its Senate, organized by academic year, with each resolution linked as a document. The archive shows what GSG has formally taken positions on over time. For 2024-2025 it lists a DEI Resolution and a Food Waste Resolution dated 09/16/2024. For 2023-2024 it lists a Student Basic Needs Resolution (01/29/2024), a USC Protecting Minors Policy Resolution (04/22/2024), a Menstrual Equity at USC resolution (04/22/2024), and an Undocumented Trojan Resource Center Resolution (04/22/2024). For 2022-2023 it lists Financial Transparency, Reliability, and Equity at USC (01/30/2023). For 2020-2021 it lists resolutions in support of fossil fuel divestment and reinvestment (11/09/2020), greater student tenant protection policies during COVID-19, CalFresh at USC campus eateries (04/12/2021), and waste-reducing practices at USC. For 2019-2020 it lists a CalFresh resolution (10/21/19), a resolution creating a Sustainability Director (10/21/19), a resolution on sexual assault and LGBTQ healthcare (4/13/20), a proposal for expanding emergency funds during COVID-19 (4/13/20), and a joint GSG and USG proposal on equitable DPS and community partnership (6/11/20). Earlier years include a proposal for a Diversity and Inclusion Council (8/21/18); resolutions on the university preferred name policy (4/16/18), the inclusion and treatment of custodial staff (4/10/18), USC Forward's unionization efforts (3/26/18), creating a university immigration task force (2/26/18), and adding Accessibility Affairs to the GSG Executive Board (11/21/17); a resolution on reinstating the Student Fee Advisory Committee and a GSG-PSOC resolution supporting refugee and Muslim targeted groups (2/13/17); resolutions on a Syria consortium, a social justice fund, and bikes (all 10/19/15); and a Black House resolution and a resolution on course evaluations (both 4/20/15). The archive page itself was last updated in April 2025, so the most recent year shown is 2024-2025.

title: How graduate students get involved in GSG
content: GSG's homepage invites students who want to get involved to learn more about the organization and its leadership opportunities, and the site offers several concrete routes. The most direct is becoming a senator: senators are elected by their peers within a particular academic department or school, represent that academic unit's recognized student organization, and are expected to dedicate 10 hours per semester. Senators then elect the GSG President and Senior Vice President and confirm Vice President and Director positions, so the senator track also leads to the Executive Board, whose 29 officers are selected every spring. A second route is volunteering on a committee: GSG's committees are made up of student volunteers with chairs elected within the committees, and the committees page publishes a sign-up form plus the expected time commitment for each, ranging from about 5-10 hours per semester for the Grants Review Committee to about 10-12 hours per semester for the Finance Committee, with roughly 8-10 hours for the Presidential Strategy and Innovation Committee and monthly one-hour meetings plus one event for the HSC Research and Development Committee. A third route is simply attending: Senate meetings are open to all, with registration information on EngageSC. Students can also join the GSG community on EngageSC, which is the prerequisite for applying to GSG grants and is where committee sign-ups and applications live. GSG's Executive Board includes a Director of Engagement and Recruitment at gsger@usc.edu for questions about joining. For most questions, GSG recommends contacting the senator for your own school or academic unit.

title: When student organizations can start booking event space
content: Trojan Event Services publishes the dates on which different groups may begin submitting reservation requests for each semester, and recognized student organizations (RSOs) always get the earliest window. For fall semester meetings and events, RSOs can submit requests starting April 1, 2026; university departments can submit starting April 24, 2026; and the open reservation period begins May 8, 2026. A restriction applies to RSOs: they cannot host events during the first three weeks of the semester, and fall events can start after September 22. For spring semester meetings and events, RSOs can submit requests starting September 15, 2026; university departments starting October 1, 2026; and the open reservation period begins October 16, 2026. Again RSOs cannot host events in the first three weeks of January, and spring events can start after January 26. For summer semester meetings and events, RSOs can submit requests starting February 1, 2027; university departments starting February 16, 2027; and the open reservation period begins March 1, 2027. Groups that need to book earlier than their first allowable date can apply for Annual Event Early Booking Status through the Annual Event Early Booking Application. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis by a committee, and approved events may request venues one year before their event date, though approval does not guarantee venue availability. The committee weighs the history of the event, the benefit to the USC community, and the necessity for early planning.

title: How recognized student organizations request campus space
content: USC Campus Activities states that recognized student organizations (RSOs) in good standing can request to book space on campus, including space in the Ronald Tutor Campus Center, outdoor venues, or classrooms, as long as the space is available, and reminds organizations to follow the policies on social events in the USC Student Handbook. To request a space, organizations submit an online reservation request on the Trojan Event Services website; questions about spaces managed by Trojan Event Services go to scevents@usc.edu. Classroom space is handled separately: groups wanting a classroom submit the Classroom Scheduling form, and Classroom Scheduling accepts requests for classroom spaces starting Week 4. Trojan Event Services confirms this division, noting that it manages only the meeting rooms in the Ronald Tutor Campus Center, while the Department of Classroom Scheduling manages all other classrooms, reachable at classroom.scheduling@usc.edu or (213) 740-4612, and has no physical office. Campus Activities lists several related RSO requirements on the same page. RSOs may not operate as businesses or generate income for individuals or businesses, and may not conduct for-profit or commercial activities or act as a front for another business or entity. RSOs may fundraise to benefit their own organization, another RSO, or an outside philanthropic agency or relief effort, but no individual may receive any benefit or payment in money, trade, discounts, or other goods or services. RSOs must submit a USC Events Permit Application (UEPA) for any event involving fundraising and must meet with Campus Activities at least two weeks beforehand for fundraising approval. Campus Activities also points RSOs to EngageSC guidance, USC Credit Union accounts for organizations in good standing, hazing prevention resources, authorized merchandise vendors, Trojans Care for Trojans, USC Report and Response, and a DPS Party Notification Form for notifying public safety about an upcoming party.

title: Reserving Ronald Tutor Campus Center meeting rooms
content: The Ronald Tutor Campus Center (TCC) houses over twenty meeting and event spaces, ranging from rooms for six people to a Grand Ballroom seating 800. Reservation requests must be submitted at least three weeks in advance, through a published online request form, and all staffing requests must be submitted at least four weeks in advance. Outside organizations must provide a certificate of insurance naming USC Trojan Event Services as additional insured. One important routing rule: USC Private Events and Conferences operates and manages reservation requests for the Trojan Grand Ballroom, the Franklin Room Suite (TCC 350, 351, and 352), and the Forum (TCC 450) for USC departments, administrative departments, and non-university clients, who should email private.events@usc.edu or call (213) 740-5956; USC recognized student organizations continue to book through the Trojan Event Services reservation request. For general information, contact the TCC Office at scevents@usc.edu or (213) 764-4943. Building hours in fall and spring are Monday to Friday 7am to 11:30pm and Saturday to Sunday 9am to 11:30pm, closed on home football games and holidays; summer hours are Monday to Friday 7am to 5:30pm with weekends closed. Offices are open Monday to Friday 9AM to 5PM, and for day-of assistance with an event in progress the number is (213) 821-7822, which is also the number to call if a TCC meeting room is locked. Students can email scevents@usc.edu with their availability to book a walk-through of a room with a production manager. The reservable rooms are TCC 221, TCC 227 (Rosen Family Screening Room), TCC 232, TCC 320A (MAAA Cruz Family Board Room), TCC 320B, TCC 320C (Hui Conference Room), TCC 350/351/352 (Franklin Suites), TCC 432 (Gupta Meeting Room), TCC 433, TCC 434, and TCC 450 (The Forum). The page also links the Facilities Planning and Management checklist and the University Event Permit Application. Separately, the Campus Center is open until midnight every day with a dedicated lounge and hallway seating on every floor for studying.

title: TCC room rates for student organizations, staffing rates, and capacities
content: Trojan Event Services publishes a rate table for Ronald Tutor Campus Center meeting rooms. Every listed TCC room is free for student organizations on a per-booking basis: TCC 221, 227, 232, 320A, 320B, 320C, 350, 351, 352, the 350+351 and 351+352 combinations, the full 350/351/352 suite, 432, 433, 434, and 450. USC departments pay hourly, free for several rooms but $100 for TCC 227 and $85 for TCC 232 and 320A, with Franklin Suite and Forum rates quoted on request; non-USC clients pay $50 to $125 hourly depending on the room. Staffing is charged separately and is not free for student organizations: an Event Staff Manager costs $34 per hour for a student organization ($39 for a USC department, $49 for non-USC clients), an Audio Technician $27 per hour ($31 / $39), and a Media (A/V) Technician $30 per hour ($34 / $43). Staffing requests must be submitted at least four weeks in advance. Capacities: TCC 221 holds 10, TCC 227 holds 72, TCC 232 holds 28, TCC 320A holds 20, TCC 320B holds 10, TCC 320C holds 6, TCC 432 holds 20, and TCC 433 and 434 each hold 14. The Franklin rooms vary by setup: TCC 350 holds 40 auditorium, 20 classroom, 28 conference, 40 empty, 24 U-shaped; TCC 351 holds 50 auditorium, 30 classroom, 28 conference, 50 empty, 24 U-shaped; TCC 352 matches TCC 350. Combining rooms, 350+351 or 351+352 each hold 90 auditorium, 60 classroom, 40 conference, 90 empty, 32 U-shaped, and the full 350/351/352 suite holds 126 auditorium, 72 classroom, 48 conference, 140 empty, 45 U-shaped. TCC 450, the Forum, holds 132 auditorium, 74 classroom, 92 for dinner rectangles, and 144 empty. Separately, the Trojan Grand Ballroom venue rental fee is discounted once per academic year for a recognized student organization, for up to 10 hours; the discount covers the venue rental fee only, cannot be combined with more than one RSO, and does not discount staffing fees.

title: RSO tabling on Trousdale Parkway and Gavin Herbert Plaza
content: Trojan Event Services defines tabling as a table in an approved campus outdoor area used to distribute information, promote events, recruit, or fundraise, and states that only recognized student organizations may table on USC campuses. Rules: RSO tabling may happen only in specific outdoor campus locations, between 10:00 a.m. and 2:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. At the University Park Campus, tabling is allowed only on Trousdale Parkway along the western edge of Alumni Park and on Gavin Herbert Plaza; tables cannot be set up on the grassy median or on the Bovard (west) side of Trousdale, and tabling is not allowed at USC Village. A valid permit is required, and the permit is non-transferable and must be displayed on the table at all times, even if the organization brings its own table and chairs. Tabling is not permitted during official university functions or holidays, including Welcome Week, Orientation, and home football game days, or when a reservation such as a career fair is using all of Trousdale. The table must be for display purposes only; a student-organization-sponsored fundraiser requires a university event permit application for fundraising approval, and the event permit requires a reservation number provided by Trojan Event Services. Setup may include a table and two chairs only, no canopy or tent, no activations, and no amplification. Up to 5 tables and 10 chairs may be borrowed from the SKS building per day. Logistics: permits are issued at the Concierge Desk on the first floor of the Steven and Kathryn Sample (SKS) building, where students give their student ID and the organization name and leave the ID at the front desk; tables are checked out from the Campus Center Consultants at the SKS front desk against a USC student ID. The permit, table, and chairs must be returned to the front desk by 2:15 p.m., or the organization risks suspension of tabling privileges or a fine equal to replacement cost; the student ID is returned on return of the equipment. An organization may table two consecutive days per week and may not exceed six days per month. Students cannot set up their own table on Trousdale if all are booked, but can add their name to a waiting list at the Campus Center Main Lobby in Sample Hall on the day; a table not picked up within an hour of its reserved time is released to the list.

title: Permits and policies that apply to student organization events
content: Several USC permits and policies apply on top of a venue reservation. A Division 5 permit is required if an event involves an open flame, or tents, canopies, or membrane structures larger than 450 square feet; Trojan Event Services publishes the LAFD Division 5 permit form. Events involving minors must follow USC's Protecting Minors Policy, which requires registering with the Office of Youth Protection and Programming 60 days before the anticipated event date; a copy of the registration form and the office's approval must go to the Trojan Event Services production manager. A blood drive requires reserving the space and completing the university event permit application. Props must be reviewed and approved by the USC Department of Public Safety and the Office of Risk Management: the organizer must notify the venue manager, complete a University Event Permit Application indicating props, identify each prop and its purpose, and upload clear photos, with all requests received two weeks before the event; props must be non-metallic, a physical inspection may be required, and no weapons of any kind are allowed on campus. Amplified sound outdoors must be requested on the Outdoor Reservation Request form and approved by Trojan Event Services, and no two events may have amplified sound at the same time. Since July 1, 2022 the university prohibits single-use plastic beverage containers on campus, USC funds may not be used to buy beverages in them, and organizers must ensure contracted event planners and caterers comply. Smoking is prohibited in all indoor and outdoor facilities on university-owned and leased property with no exception, including vehicles parked there and recognized fraternity and sorority property, and the definition covers cigarettes, cigars, pipes, e-cigarettes, hookah, and any lit product; event organizers are responsible for enforcing the Smoke Free Policy at their events and must have a plan of action for violations, which may include hiring Allied Universal Security or training volunteers, and failure to act on a reported or witnessed violation may result in losing the ability to host future events. Decorations require Trojan Event Services approval at least two weeks before the event and must be removed immediately afterward or cleaning fees apply; taping, stapling, gluing or otherwise attaching items to walls, doors, curtains, windows, posts, columns, floors or ceilings is prohibited, as are glitter and confetti, fog and bubble machines, and candles, flames of any kind, and pyrotechnics. Candles must be LED. Flyer posting is prohibited on trees and hedges, the ground, buildings, elevators, statues including Tommy Trojan, trash and recycling cans, lamp posts, fences, utility poles, parking structures, over other posted materials, fountains, by chalking, on cars or bicycles, and as freestanding signs; the full policy is in the USC Student Handbook, Appendix IX. Tailgate permits are handled at gameday.usc.edu, and Trojan Event Services does not reserve outdoor spaces on home football game days.

title: Event payments, deposits, cancellations, furniture, and catering
content: Payments: Trojan Event Services accepts cash for payments under $50, all major credit cards, internal requisitions (IR), cashier's checks, and money orders, but no personal checks.
